# Clinical, molecular, and immune characterization of naturally occurring osteosarcoma in dogs (COTC034)

  * Recruiting
  * Dog
  * Oncology

The purpose of this study is to better understand the biology of primary bone cancer of the leg (appendicular osteosarcoma, OS) in dogs. This is a common cancer that occurs in dogs and it is often closely compared to OS in humans (primarily adolescents). The standard approach to treating dogs with OS is amputation of the affected leg, followed by chemotherapy. In this case, half the dogs have spread of OS to the lungs within 6 months despite amputation and chemotherapy, and half have died of disease by 10-11 months. Only a small proportion of dogs are long term survivors, living beyond 2 years. There is an increasing effort to study new treatments in pet dogs with OS to develop better, more effective therapies for both people and pets. This is known as comparative and translational canine cancer research. However, a big challenge for this effort is that we still don’t completely understand the natural biology of OS in dogs...that is, we don’t; know what happens when dogs with OS undergo amputation alone (i.e., no chemotherapy).

## 5. Conclusions

Some studies were focused on validating gene transfer and expression methods by treating few patients with different kinds of tumors in the same study where the heterogeneity and the absence of control groups precluded conclusions about the efficacy of the treatment. Nevertheless, these studies were valuable as feasibility, proof of concept, and safety assessment.

On the other hand, larger studies involving higher numbers of patients with the same kind of tumor, often with suitable control groups, were able to generate statistically significant data to validate the efficacy of the proposed treatments.

For biosafety reasons (concerning both animals and humans), as well as the higher cost of viral vector production, most veterinary cancer gene therapy protocols have relied on non-viral vectors, with electrotransfer being the predominant delivery method from 2017 to 2024.

To date, more than 2054 clinical protocols for gene therapy for cancer have been registered [70], resulting in 20 treatments approved worldwide for marketing, according to the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy (ASGCT). In veterinary oncology, the situation is much more modest, with around a hundred publications on the subject and only two treatments approved for commercialization: a plasmid vector with the human tyrosinase gene as a xenoantigen for canine melanoma (Oncept™ Canine Melanoma Vaccine, Duluth, GA, USA) and a canarypox virus vector with the feline interleukin-2 gene for feline fibrosarcoma (Oncept IL-2™).

Almost three decades have passed since the first report with clinical results of the application of genetic immunotherapy in companion animals [1]. Despite proposals for the implementation of veterinary clinical protocols for cancer therapies with a translational approach [6,7,8,71], the treatments approved so far for humans were not previously tested in companion animals.

On the other hand, some complex treatment approaches for autologous that involve genetic modifications of ex vivo cells, first went through clinical studies in humans than in companion animals. Although they may have high translational value, these technologies are currently very expensive to be applied in veterinary medicine.

Oncolytic virotherapy is emerging as a new tool against cancer in companion animals [72,73]. The update of those approaches that only used suicide genes and/or oncolytic viruses in companion animals would deserve a separate review.

In veterinary medicine, non-viral vectors probably offer a better opportunity to treat animal tumors in a more affordable way for owners. Greater investment in time and effort will be necessary to validate the results in prospective controlled studies and ultimately offer immunogene therapy to more patients who currently lack effective treatment options.

# BG34-200 plus immunotherapy for canine malignant melanoma

  * Suspended
  * Dog
  * Oncology

The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of a new cancer immune therapy, BG34-200, for the treatment of canine malignant melanoma, alone or in combination with other agents that work to stimulate the immune system. BG34-200 is a new immune stimulant derived from oat bran that activates a specific set of immune cells called monocytes and macrophages. These cells are an important part of the tumor environment and can work to either stimulate or block the immune system’s ability to kill cancer cells. In mice, BG34-200 was able to shrink several different kinds of tumors. The current study will build on these findings to test how effective BG34-200 is in the setting of cancer in dogs.

The potential benefit to your dog is that the BG34-200 treatment with or without the other immune stimulants treatment will activate your dog’s immune system and shrink the tumor or prevent the tumor from growing any further.

# SBRT for Canine Lung Tumor Study

  * Recruiting
  * Dog
  * Oncology

Primary pulmonary carcinomas in dogs are most commonly treated with surgery, which can result in survival times of approximately one year. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) is a highly precise form of radiation therapy that delivers high doses of radiation directly to a tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding normal tissues. The purpose of this study is to evaluate dogs with primary pulmonary carcinoma treated using a standardized SBRT protocol across institutions participating in the Veterinary Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (VRTOG).

## Inclusion Criteria

Dogs are eligible for enrollment if they meet all of the following criteria:

  * Cytologic or histopathologic diagnosis of a single primary pulmonary carcinoma.
  * Primary lung tumor measuring greater than 1 cm in its shortest diameter.
  * No previous treatment for the lung tumor.
  * No diagnosis of another malignant tumor outside the lungs within 30 days before enrollment.

### 临床招募｜犬三类肿瘤新药免费临床试验

2026-08-18

Image

家里狗狗确诊肥大细胞瘤、骨肉瘤、口腔鳞癌？

各位接诊此类病例的宠物医师请注意！

中农董军实验室抗肿瘤新药临床试验正式开启全国招募，符合条件的患病犬可免费使用抗肿瘤新药。

本次临床试验，既能大幅减轻宠物主人高额用药的经济压力，同时也会为犬类肿瘤治疗研发更安全有效的全新方案。

诚邀全国宠物医生积极推荐适配病例，也欢迎患病犬主咨询报名，推动小动物肿瘤诊疗水平持续提升。

* * *

三大实验组招募（名额有限）

试验组1：犬肥大细胞瘤

本次试验为新药初步临床效果研究，通过规范给药、定期复查监测，客观评估抗肿瘤药物对犬肥大细胞瘤的临床效果治疗新方案。

肿瘤状态：复发/未切除

试验组2：犬骨肉瘤

本次试验为新药初步临床效果研究，通过规范给药、定期复查监测，客观评估抗肿瘤药物对骨肉瘤的临床效果治疗新方案。

肿瘤状态：未截肢/肺部转移

试验组3：犬口腔鳞癌

本次试验为新药初步临床效果研究，通过规范给药、定期复查监测，客观评估抗肿瘤药物对口腔鳞癌的临床效果治疗新方案。

参与福利

1.试验周期内，抗肿瘤新药免费使用，无需承担药费；

2.全程实验室专业技术团队跟进，定期免费肿瘤相关指标复查、病灶评估；

犬只入组要求（带瘤病例）

1.确诊依据：经组织病理检测确诊为肥大细胞瘤 / 骨肉瘤 / 口腔鳞癌（需提供病理报告）；

2.年龄：1 岁以上，无严重心肝肾衰竭、重度贫血等终末期基础重病；

3.主人配合度：可按要求按时送犬复查、配合采血、病灶影像学记录，完整完成全试验周期；

试验流程

1.报名登记：医师 / 主人联系对接人，提交病理报告、犬只基础病历；

2.初筛评估：实验室审核病例，确认符合入组标准后通知；

3.基线检查：入组前完成基础血液、肿瘤病灶基线检测；

4.规范给药：按照试验方案免费提供新药， 院内给药；

5.定期随访复查：固定周期检测病灶大小、血液指标，记录药物反应与肿瘤情况；

# Register your interest in our dog cancer trial

We are recruiting dogs with mast cell cancer in Australia for an investigational trial of personalised mRNA cancer vaccines. Register your interest and share a few details about your dog. Our team will contact you about further screening.

Why we are running this trial

## From Rosie’s story to a future for more dogs.

Image: Rosie

Rosie

The first dog treated with a personalised neoantigen vaccine.

It began with Rosie. Her experience with a personalised neoantigen vaccine encouraged Paul to explore how this approach could one day be made available to every dog with cancer.

Before an approach like this can become broadly available, we must study it carefully and support it by evidence for review by the relevant veterinary regulators. This clinical trial is an important step in that process, helping us learn from participating dogs and understand the vaccine more fully.

Read Rosie’s personalised mRNA cancer-vaccine story  →

Who can register

## If your dog has cancer and is currently in Australia, you’re welcome to register your interest. Our team will check whether your dog may be eligible for this trial.

Register your interest  →

About the trial

## What this trial is looking at

The trial will investigate a personalised mRNA vaccine approach for dogs with mast cell cancer. Tell us about your dog and our team will help determine whether they may be eligible for screening.

Image

### Who can register

Dogs diagnosed with mast cell cancer who are based in, or able to travel within, Australia.

Every case is reviewed individually

Image

### The trial approach

A therapeutic mRNA vaccine designed from each dog’s own tumour and blood samples, intended to work alongside—not replace—existing care.

Personalised to each dog

Image

### What screening involves

We help coordinate records, screening, sample logistics and updates, working with the trial team and your treating veterinarian.

A named team stays in touch

Trial registration and screening

## How to register your interest.

You don’t need to have every record ready before registering your interest. Start with what you know and we’ll help with the rest.

01

### Register your interest

Complete a short form with basic details about your dog, their mast cell cancer diagnosis and where you live.

02

### We get in touch

A Gamgee coordinator will contact you, answer practical questions and—with your permission—help gather relevant records from your vet.

03

### The trial team confirms eligibility

The authorised study team and treating veterinarian assess potential eligibility. If your dog may proceed, you’ll receive the approved trial information and consent discussion before deciding.

These are indicative timings from a single case. Sequencing turnaround and manufacturing schedules may vary. We will give you a case-specific estimate before proceeding.

## Ready to tell us about your dog?

Registering your interest does not guarantee eligibility or enrolment. Please continue your dog's existing veterinary care while your information is reviewed.

Register your interest  →

Purpose of study: 

To assess efficacy and safety of Kv9 across a range of solid tumours.

  * Tumour type diagnosed by fine needle aspirate or biopsy by a registered veterinary pathologist 

  * ​Tumour smaller than 5cm 

  * Not receiving immune modulatory drugs

    * It is acceptable to be taking/receiving including apoquel, cytopoint, beranza or a recent vaccination

    * Other tumour types will be a case by case basis ​

  1. Primary veterinarian to send through referral for assessment by Kode Veterinary Sciences (KVS). 

  2. Additional testing completed as required. 

  3. Atleast two treatment appointments to receive Kv9 at treatment centres.

  4. A minimum of 9 revisits at primary care veterinarian or treatment centres over 2 years.

  * You are responsible to schedule and attend all required visits  ​

  * You are responsible for the initial costs to diagnose your dogs tumour, and any other tests recommended by your veterinarian

Only the treating veterinary team can advise whether surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy, palliative care or a research study is appropriate for an individual dog.

Is there a cancer vaccine for dogs?

Yes, although there is no single vaccine for every type of canine cancer. Gamgee is developing a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine for dogs, created using information from each dog’s own tumor. The approach is currently investigational and is being studied through an Australian clinical trial.

Does a dog cancer vaccine prevent cancer?

Most cancer vaccines for dogs are therapeutic, meaning they are intended for dogs that already have cancer. Gamgee is currently studying this type of vaccine: a personalized mRNA vaccine designed from each dog’s tumor. Preventive cancer vaccines are also being researched, but they are not part of Gamgee’s current trial.

Is an mRNA cancer vaccine available for dogs?

Personalized mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs remain investigational. Gamgee is evaluating its approach through an Australian clinical trial currently limited to mast cell tumor and osteosarcoma. Registration does not guarantee screening, eligibility, enrollment or treatment.

If enrolled in the study, your pet will receive several small injections (less than 0.2mL at each site) of a Kv9 solution directly into their tumour mass every 14 days for up to three occasions. ... Kv9 is an experimental treatment and cannot be guaranteed to cure cancer.
Most side effects are mild and temporary, such as tiredness, reduced appetite, or swelling at the tumour site.

### Will this cure my pet?

Kv9 is an experimental treatment and cannot be guaranteed to cure cancer. The goal is to slow or stop tumour growth while maintaining good quality of life.

### Does it cost anything to participate in the trial?

No, the Kv9 treatment is provided at no cost and necessary veterinary visits during the clinical study are covered by KVS. To be eligible for the clinical study your pet must have their tumour diagnosed by your primary care veterinarian, this is at your own cost. KVS will provide support if there are changes in your pet suspected to be caused by participating in the trial, this is often including financial support. Any changes that are not suspected to be related to the trial or have been previously agreed upon to be excluded such as pre-exisiting conditions will be the owners responsibility to seek veterinary advice and manage.

### Can I withdraw my pet?

Yes, participation is voluntary, and you may withdraw your pet from the trial at any time without penalty.

### How long does each treatment appointment take?

Treatment appointments may take up to 30 minutes followed by a 20 minute waiting time. Monitoring appointments may take up to 15 minutes.

### How long will my pet be in the trial?

The trial participation last just over 2 years. This includes the treatment visits in the first month, and 9 follow up visits over the following 2 years.

### What approvals have you obtained to run this study?

KVS has approval from the Ministry of Primary Industries and an external animal ethics committee to run this study.

In 2024, Rosie was diagnosed with mast cell cancer. ... I started researching, using AI to map the specific mutations driving her cancer, design a personalised mRNA vaccine targeting those mutations, and coordinate its manufacture with researchers at UNSW. ... Explore Our Vaccine → Learn About Our Trial → ... Personalised mRNA vaccine plus supporting protocol.
The underlying tools already exist: genomic sequencing, protein modelling and mRNA synthesis. What I built for Rosie was not new science. It was a new route to access.

I should not have been the only person who could do this. A background in machine learning and months of obsessive research should not be the price of admission. Every dog owner facing this diagnosis deserves the same options I had, without having to become a citizen scientist to get them.

Where we are right now

## The first end-to-end personalised cancer treatment protocol for dogs.

# Available Canine Brain Tumor Trials

## Trial #1: Investigating the safety and efficacy of combining Zika virus vaccines and autologous tumor lysates in pet dogs with high-grade gliomas

### About

This trial focuses on providing a thoroughly tested vaccine against a virus called Zika virus alongside vaccines created directly from a dog's own brain tumor cells. Tumors are removed surgically. Enrolled dogs receive vaccines twice before surgery, then three times after surgery. These vaccines can be performed by local veterinary teams. Every 16 weeks, MRIs are performed to monitor treatment response.

### Enrollment requirements

All dogs with MRI-confirmed gliomas are eligible for enrollment in this trial. Dogs must be amenable to handling. Prior to enrollment, dogs must be screened for any evidence of cancer in their thorax (chest) or abdomen.

### Covered costs

  * All costs associated with surgery, post-operative MRI, post-operative care, and infusions are covered by the study
  * Clients must pay for pre-enrollment thoracic (chest) and abdominal radiographs (X-rays), and for the MRI that is performed to diagnose their dog's brain tumor

Enroll in Trial Email with questions

## Trial #2: Using nanoparticles to deliver anti-tumor genes to pet dogs with high-grade gliomas

### About

This trial focuses on delivering anti-tumor genes directly to the tumor by attaching them to nanoparticles that the tumor cells ingest. Tumors are removed surgically, then the nanoparticle medication is used to line the cavity. Every 16 weeks, MRIs are performed to monitor treatment response.

### Enrollment requirements

All dogs with MRI-confirmed gliomas are eligible for enrollment in this trial. Dogs must be amenable to handling. Prior to enrollment, dogs must be screened for any evidence of cancer in their thorax (chest) or abdomen.

### Covered costs

  * All costs associated with surgery, post-operative MRI, post-operative care, and infusions are covered by the study
  * Clients must pay for pre-enrollment thoracic (chest) and abdominal radiographs (X-rays), and for the MRI that is performed to diagnose their dog's brain tumor

Enroll in trial

# Advancing Canine Brain Tumor Treatment

## What We Do

The Canine Brain Tumor Program provides advanced clinical care for dogs while accelerating human brain tumor research.

## About the program

The University of Minnesota Canine Brain Tumor Program is a multifaceted, internationally recognized program that advances care for both dogs and people affected by primary brain tumors. We provide cutting-edge therapy to dogs to preserve their quality of life and improve long-term survival. We study how canine and human gliomas are similar to each other, so that the clinical trials we conduct benefit both dogs and people. Our trials are supported by a variety of financial sponsors, including grants from foundations and government agencies. The majority of costs associated with enrollment are covered through these funding mechanisms.

## Join our clinical trials

Enroll now

## Collaborate with us

The CBTP partners with scientific organizations conducting cutting edge clinical research. Our goal is to unite canine brain tumor patients with innovative diagnostic and treatment options. To learn more about collaborating with the CBTP, please contact us at [email protected].

## Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my dog has a brain tumor?

Every dog is different. Some dogs with brain tumors develop seizures. Others experience personality changes or difficulty walking. The issues can develop quickly or can get worse slowly over time.

What types of brain tumors qualify for the trials?

Currently, we enroll dogs with gliomas in our clinical trials. These are primary brain tumors, meaning that they develop from inside the brain itself. We can make an educated guess of whether a dog has a glioma or a different tumor based on the appearance of the tumor on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

How do we get our dog enrolled in a trial?

If you suspect your dog may have a brain tumor, the first step is to have your dog evaluated by a veterinary neurologist, who can perform an MRI on your dog's brain. If the MRI shows a tumor that appears to be a glioma, then your dog may qualify for one of our clinical trials. Either you or your dog's neurologist can then contact the CBTP at [email protected]. A CBTP team member will guide you through the process from there. Expect to be asked to provide medical records and your dog's MRI for us to review. Then, Dr. Arnold will arrange a phone call with you to discuss the clinical trial process.

L18: At this time, the study is open to dogs with confirmed osteosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma, and transitional cell carcinoma.

L20: The vaccine is currently provided to the study sites and owner at no charge. As this is not a fully funded study, all costs associated with evaluation, testing, and vaccine administration are the responsibility of the owner.
L21: ##### General Study Enrollment Criteria
L22: 
L23: • Histologically (biopsy) confirmed diagnosis of osteosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma, or transitional cell carcinoma. An exception may be made if the dog has a long bone (limb) lesion consistent with osteosarcoma and the owner has elected not to pursue amputation. If amputation is planned, the first dose of vaccine can be administered following the amputation.
L24: 
L25: • Anticipated survival of 3 months as determined by the evaluating oncologist.
L26: • While dogs with metastases may be enrolled in the study, this will be based on the extent/volume of disease and prognosis.
